title: We swapped landed living for a 2,200 sq ft condo. Is a big apartment a better family home?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #245 | SUPER HAPPY WITH HER HOME PURCHASE
excerpt: A mother who left multi-storey landed homes for a five-room condo near Sungai Long is delighted. Sean compares large apartments with terrace houses, and explains how to read price per sq ft.

qa.asker: W, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: W lived in landed homes in Cheras for 40 years, first her parents' three-storey house and then her in-laws' two-storey one, which were hot under the roof and kept her children upstairs and apart. In 2020 she bought a 2,200 sq ft condo at about RM335 per sq ft, with five rooms, five bathrooms and an extended terrace facing a golf course near Sungai Long. She is delighted with the space, the breeze and having no stairs.
qa.question: How does a large apartment compare with a landed house as a family home?
qa.quote: What we want is daylight; what we don't want is sunlight.
qa.answer: For many families a large apartment lives better than a terrace house: one level, no stairs, cooler rooms and facilities for the children, at a price close to a comparable terrace in the city. Landed homes still win on parking right at the door, freedom to renovate and, so far, capital growth.

reasons.title: Compare price per square foot like for like
reasons.body: Bigger units always have a lower price per square foot, which is why developers quote the largest unit's figure. Compare new with new and similar sizes, such as 2,000 to 2,500 sq ft units with each other, before judging a price.

reasons.title: One level suits young children and ageing knees
reasons.body: In a three-storey house the staircase takes about 18% to 20% of the built-up area, and families end up split between floors. A single level makes night feeds, keeping an eye on children and getting older much easier.

reasons.title: Orientation decides how hot it gets
reasons.body: Walls facing the evening sun soak up heat and release it at night. Sean wants daylight, not direct sun, so he prefers east over west when those are the only choices; terrace houses with roofs fully exposed are usually hotter than flats.

reasons.title: Renovation and growth differ
reasons.body: Condos can't be structurally changed, so a renovation budget goes further. Landed houses still lead capital growth in NAPIC data, though large units in Kuala Lumpur rent well; Sean says a large Mont Kiara unit furnished by The Makeover Guys rents for RM13,000 to RM15,000.

actions: Compare a unit's price per square foot only with units of similar size and age nearby.
Picture daily routines, such as groceries, children and older parents, in both a condo and a landed home before choosing.
Check which way the main rooms and balcony face; avoid units that take the full evening sun.
Budget for the condo's higher maintenance fee against a landed home's irregular upkeep, such as painting and gates.
Plan ahead: a large condo can be rented out when the children leave and you downsize.
qa.caveat: Landed living is easier when you go to and from the car often, and remains Sean's pick for capital growth. His view that large apartments may become the better investment is a hypothesis he hasn't proven.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #245. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Prices are as Sean stated them in March 2024. The episode was sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company Sean works with; he says he also rents one of their furnished units.
